content.title: Probability in Frequency Tables, Two-Way Tables, and Set Relationships
content.overview: This lesson focuses on how to extract data and calculate probabilities from frequency tables, two-way tables, and set relationships (such as Venn diagrams). On the SAT, correctly identifying the sample space (denominator) and the target event (numerator) is the key to solving these problems.
learning_objectives: Extract frequencies for specific categories from frequency tables and calculate simple probabilities.
Interpret two-way tables and calculate conditional probabilities based on rows, columns, or totals.
Use set relationships (such as Venn diagrams) to identify overlapping regions and calculate probabilities.
Distinguish between probability calculations for "all participants" versus "specific subgroups."

sections.title: Frequency Tables and Basic Probability
sections.content: A frequency table shows the number of times different categories occur. The basic formula for calculating probability is: $P(E) = \frac{\text{Frequency of target event}}{\text{Total frequency}}$. When working with frequency tables, be sure to first confirm whether the question asks for the "entire sample" or a "specific subset."

sections.title: Two-Way Tables and Conditional Probability
sections.content:
Two-way tables are used to show the relationship between two categorical variables. The intersection of a row and a column represents the frequency of individuals who satisfy both conditions simultaneously. When calculating conditional probability, the sample space narrows. For example, if a question asks "Of the students who chose A, what is the probability they chose B?", the denominator should only be the "total number of students who chose A," not the grand total of the entire table.

![Steps for Calculating Conditional Probability](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/073c76c2-8aa4-4ca5-b4d1-5f113c935822-1786502076507-996.webp)

sections.title: Set Relationships and Venn Diagrams
sections.content: Set relationships usually involve "and" (intersection) and "or" (union). In a Venn diagram, the middle overlapping part represents individuals who satisfy both conditions. When calculating the probability of "A or B," the formula is: $P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)$. Subtracting the intersection avoids double-counting the individuals in the overlapping section.

worked_examples.question:
The table below shows the sports preferences of students in a class:
| | Likes Basketball | Does Not Like Basketball | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Likes Soccer | 12 | 8 | 20 |
| Does Not Like Soccer | 5 | 10 | 15 |
| Total | 17 | 18 | 35 |
If a student is chosen at random from those who like soccer, what is the probability that the student also likes basketball?
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Determine the sample space (denominator). The question asks to choose "from those who like soccer," so the denominator is the total number of people who like soccer, which is 20.
Step 2: Determine the target event (numerator). Among those who like soccer, the number of people who also like basketball is 12.
Step 3: Calculate the probability. $P = \frac{12}{20} = \frac{3}{5}$ or 0.6.

common_mistakes: Denominator Error: Incorrectly using the grand total of the table as the denominator when calculating conditional probability instead of the restricted subgroup total.
Double Counting: Forgetting to subtract the intersection when calculating the probability of a union (A or B), leading to a probability higher than the actual value.
Table Reading Error: Confusing the locations of row totals and column totals.
exam_tips: Carefully read qualifiers in the question such as "Given that..." or "Of those who...", as these words usually indicate the scope of the denominator.
If the question asks for the answer as a percentage, remember to multiply the fraction or decimal by 100.
In a two-way table, check that the sum of the row totals equals the sum of the column totals to ensure the data is understood correctly.
content.recap: The key to mastering frequency tables and two-way tables lies in accurately locating the numerator (the specific frequency meeting the condition) and the denominator (the reference group defined by the question). For set problems, always be careful to remove duplicates from overlapping sections.

knowledge_claims.content: A frequency table is a table that records the number of occurrences of each category in a dataset.
A two-way table is used to summarize data for two categorical variables, showing the interaction between them.
To calculate simple probability, divide the frequency of the target category by the total frequency of the sample.
In a two-way table, the intersection of the row totals and column totals represents the total quantity of the entire sample.
When calculating conditional probability, the sample space (denominator) must be restricted to the subgroup specified in the question.
Phrases such as "Given that" or "Of the [category]" in a question usually imply that it is a conditional probability problem.
The formula for calculating the probability of the union of two sets is $P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)$.
When calculating the probability of "A or B," failing to subtract the intersection $P(A \text{ and } B)$ results in double-counting individuals in the overlapping section.
The overlapping region in a Venn diagram represents the frequency of individuals who satisfy two or more conditions simultaneously.
In a two-way table, the sum of the frequencies of all internal cells must equal the grand total value in the bottom-right corner.
